item.title: Psychology Daily · November 11, 2026
item.description: Today's thread is that broad labels are being broken into measurable pieces. PMDD is not one condition but three subtypes with different onsets; the value of an antidepressant is not only how fast it works but whether it holds; and the chain from gender norms to distress mostly breaks in the middle in 1,651 adolescents. The finer the classification, the more specific the point of intervention. 1,651 Ethiopian adolescents: most direct paths from gender norms to distress did not hold

item.title: Psychology Daily · November 10, 2026
item.description: All five stories today sit in the same narrow band: the effect is real, it is small, and almost every design is missing the one feature that would settle it. One lost hour of sleep adds two points to a phishing click rate. Across 14 countries, shouting and hitting both travel with toddler behaviour problems, but not in a direction the data can fix. A choir for 14 children has no comparison group. A 145-patient emergency-department model has just nine positive cases in its 30-patient clinician comparison. Small is not the same as useless — but it does decide who should pay for the fix, and how much it is worth. One hour less sleep moved simulated phishing clicks from 15.56% to 17.76%

item.title: Psychology Daily · November 9, 2026
item.description: Today's thread is that psychological states are becoming readable signals — and readability is not the same as usefulness. A 92-country survey of 53,799 people puts the lows among young adults and richer countries; the full Instagram archives of 415 students separate emotional from social loneliness; and Wuhan has turned “work smell” into an eight-department clinic that saw 30,000 visits in three months. The more signals we have, the more insistently the same question returns: does any of this change an outcome? A 92-country survey of 53,799 people: mental wealth is lowest among the young and in richer countries
